Credit-card cash back: chart the category cap, the annual fee and the interest

Compare two hypothetical cash-back cards using the same existing purchases, then test category eligibility, spending caps and annual costs without increasing the household budget.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Explore cash-back categories, a cap and annual costs

Interactive planning lab

Premium card: gross cash back$432
Premium card: cash back less fee and interest$312
Premium advantage over the no-fee comparison$72

Invented cash-back terms for the same existing purchases on two hypothetical cards. Bonus eligibility is capped by annual purchase dollars; excess bonus-category purchases earn the base rate. All rewards are redeemed at their entered cash value. The same independently entered interest amount is deducted from both choices, without calculating actual interest, grace periods or repayment. No new spending, points valuation, merchant surcharge, welcome offer or additional benefits are modeled.

On this page

  1. Keep the purchase budget fixed before comparing rewards
  2. Apply the category cap before multiplying by the reward rate
  3. Separate gross cash back from the net result

The central idea

A higher advertised reward rate applies only to eligible purchases on the stated terms. Compare the cash actually earned with the fee and interest, using spending the household already intended to make.

01

Keep the purchase budget fixed before comparing rewards

A rewards comparison starts with purchases the household already plans to make. Increasing spending to reach a reward threshold creates a new expense as well as a reward. These charts therefore hold an existing annual budget fixed when comparing the two hypothetical cards.

The example uses CAD 24,000 of eligible annual purchases. Forty percent, or CAD 9,600, belongs to a bonus category. The premium card pays an assumed 3% on qualifying purchases up to an annual purchase-dollar cap, and 1% on the remainder. It charges a CAD 120 annual fee. The comparison card charges no annual fee and pays 1% on all those purchases.

The FCAC’s credit-card guide identifies rates, fees and rewards as important comparison features and notes that interest can reduce reward value. No actual card, approval criterion, merchant classification or offered reward rate is used here. The terms are original teaching assumptions.

02

Apply the category cap before multiplying by the reward rate

The premium card’s annual cap is CAD 10,000 of purchases eligible for its bonus rate. Under the default mix, bonus purchases are CAD 9,600, so the cap does not yet bind. Those purchases earn CAD 288. The remaining CAD 14,400 earns CAD 144 at the 1% base rate.

Total gross cash back is therefore CAD 432. The no-fee card earns CAD 240 on the same CAD 24,000 of purchases. The gross difference is CAD 192, but that is before the premium card’s CAD 120 annual fee. Its advantage after the fee is CAD 72 in this invented example.

If the bonus-category share rises to 50%, the household has CAD 12,000 of purchases in that category. Only CAD 10,000 earns 3%; the remaining CAD 2,000 earns the base rate along with other purchases. The category-mix line therefore stops gaining an additional bonus once the cap is reached. An annual purchase cap is different from a limit on the cash reward itself.

03

Separate gross cash back from the net result

The waterfall begins with the two cash-back components and subtracts the annual fee. At zero entered interest, its endpoint is CAD 312. That amount is gross cash back of CAD 432 less the CAD 120 fee; it is not the same as the CAD 72 advantage over another card that also earns rewards.

The annual interest input is an independently entered cash cost. It is applied equally to both cards, so the comparison does not silently give one card a different repayment pattern. If CAD 400 is entered, the premium card’s net reward becomes negative CAD 88 and the no-fee card’s becomes negative CAD 160.

The premium card still has a CAD 72 relative advantage because a common CAD 400 cost cancels in the subtraction. Both absolute results are negative, however. A favourable comparison with one alternative does not mean that rewards cover all costs. The model does not calculate actual interest from statement dates, grace periods, rates or daily balances.

04

Read the spending curve as alternatives, not a target

Each point on the spending chart represents a different existing annual purchase budget with the same category share and reward terms. The line is useful for identifying where a fee is covered by incremental cash back. It does not suggest increasing spending until a preferred card wins.

With the default terms, the premium card earns two extra percentage points only on bonus-eligible purchases. Before the cap binds, a 40% bonus-category share creates an extra reward of 0.8% of total eligible purchases. Covering a CAD 120 fee therefore requires CAD 15,000 of those purchases: CAD 120 divided by 0.008.

That threshold relies on the selected mix, rates and cap. If the mix changes, or a merchant is ineligible, the calculation changes. After the CAD 10,000 bonus-purchase cap is reached, the maximum extra reward at the default rates is CAD 200 before the fee. More base-rate spending then adds the same reward to both cards.

05

Use the matrix to isolate the fee and the category mix

The matrix keeps annual eligible purchases at the selected total and varies two assumptions: the premium fee and the bonus-category share. Positive cells show a premium-card advantage under these terms; negative cells show a no-fee-card advantage. Neither colour is an assessment of a real product’s suitability.

The common interest amount does not change the matrix because it is deducted from both choices. The waterfall and line charts still show its effect on absolute net cash back. This separation helps answer two distinct questions: which entered card has the better relative result, and whether either card’s rewards exceed the entered costs.

Benefits such as travel cover, lounge access, purchase protection or introductory bonuses are excluded. Add a benefit only after confirming that it is available, useful and not already supplied elsewhere. A headline advertised value is not automatically equivalent to cash the household would otherwise spend.

06

Reconcile the model with the actual card agreement

For a real comparison, classify a supported purchase history using each issuer’s eligibility rules. Confirm whether caps apply by month, year, category or account, and whether spending above a cap receives a base rate. Review exclusions, redemption conditions, additional-card fees and any applicable merchant charges.

This model assumes every earned dollar is redeemed at its entered cash value. It does not value points, account for expiry, calculate a minimum redemption threshold or assume that a welcome offer repeats annually. These features can change the result and need their own supported amounts and dates.

Keep repayment planning separate from reward optimization. The charts compare the same purchases and an explicit cost allowance; they do not calculate a borrowing limit, a credit score or an affordable repayment. A practical comparison preserves the purchase budget, verifies the terms and checks the resulting costs in dollars before treating a reward rate as a saving.
